title: The Kilimanjaro Sundowner That Became East Africa's Flying Doctors
dek: In 1956 three surgeons talked over drinks on a Kilimanjaro farm; in 1957 they began taking surgery by air to cut-off East African hospitals.

story.founder: Michael Wood, Archibald McIndoe, Thomas Rees
story.company: African Medical and Research Foundation (later Amref Health Africa)
story.event: Founding a flying surgical service and radio network for remote East African hospitals
story.summary: In 1956, at Ol Orien farm on the slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro, the reconstructive surgeons Michael Wood, Archibald McIndoe and Tom Rees first discussed taking specialist care to remote East African hospitals and linking them by radio to Nairobi. In 1957 they founded the organisation that became AMREF and its Flying Doctors, starting with a four-seater Piper Tri-Pacer, a radio network and outreach to four hospitals in remote Kenya; Wood flew the plane and worked unpaid in the early years.
paragraphs: In 1956, over sundowners at Ol Orien farm on the slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro, three reconstructive surgeons began to talk about the health of people far from any doctor. Archibald McIndoe, a New Zealander known for his reconstructive surgery on Battle of Britain pilots, owned land on the mountain. Michael Wood, who had trained under him at East Grinstead and moved to Kenya in 1948, partly for his asthma, farmed next door. The third was Tom Rees, an American and another of McIndoe's former pupils.

What they knew came from their own work. Across East Africa, by Amref's later reckoning, there was about one doctor for every 30,000 people, and small rural hospitals were cut off by hard terrain and poor communications. Among the children they saw, the Flying Doctors' own history says, three in four had burns. Their plan was to take specialist surgery to those hospitals instead of waiting for patients to reach a city, and to connect the hospitals to expert advice by a radio network with Nairobi at its centre.

In 1957 they founded the organisation that became the African Medical and Research Foundation, whose flying arm was known as the Flying Doctors. It started small: a four-seater Piper Tri-Pacer, which Wood flew himself, a budget the Flying Doctors put at $14,000, and an outreach programme serving four hospitals in remote Kenya. Rees, who practised in Manhattan, raised money in the United States with his wife Nan. In those early years Wood worked unpaid, while his wife Sue supported the family by running their farm.

Growth was slow. McIndoe died suddenly of a heart attack in 1960, the year the foundation spent only £11,500 and had three permanent staff. That year the American broadcaster Arthur Godfrey gave it a Piper Aztec and a Piper Cherokee, tripling the fleet. The first professional pilot was hired in 1961, though Wood kept flying his own plane, and the radio room, called Foundation Control, came to link more than 100 remote stations.

In 1978 a Los Angeles Times reporter flew with Wood, then 59, to a Maasai settlement south-east of Nairobi. His explanation was short: "you go to your patients. If you wait for them to come to you, they simply die."

quote.text: Be not slow to visit a sick man; for by such things thou shalt gain love.
quote.source_title: The Wisdom of the Apocrypha, Project Gutenberg eBook #77250
quote.connection: Wood's reason for flying was practical: patients who must travel to a doctor often die on the way. Ben Sira gives a second reason the story leaves out. Going to the sick without delay is also how affection and trust are earned.

reflection: The plan made over those sundowners was large, but what began in 1957 was small: one four-seater plane, four hospitals, and a founder who was not paid. The radio network and the larger fleet came later, built on what the first years proved.

You may be carrying a large plan too. It can help to ask what your version of four hospitals is: the few people near enough to visit, whose needs you can see for yourself, before you try to reach everyone. Going to them costs time. It also tells you things that no report sent to you ever will.
invitation: Choose one person who uses your work and whom you have only heard from at a distance. This week, visit or call them and ask what the hardest part of their working day is.

sources.title: Our Founders
sources.supports: The idea first raised in 1956 over sundowners at Ol Orien farm on the slopes of Mt Kilimanjaro by McIndoe, Wood and Rees; the plan to bring specialised care to rural hospitals cut off by terrain and poor communications and to link them by a radio network with Nairobi as the hub; McIndoe's wartime surgery on pilots and his farm in Tanzania; Wood's training at East Grinstead at McIndoe's invitation and move to Kenya in 1948, partly because of asthma; Wood working for nothing while Sue ran the family farm; Rees and his wife Nan fundraising in the United States; McIndoe's death from a heart attack in 1960; expenditure of only £11,500 and three permanent staff in 1960; Arthur Godfrey's gift of a Piper Aztec and a Piper Cherokee tripling the fleet; first professional pilot hired in 1961 while Wood continued to fly his own plane.

sources.title: Our History
sources.supports: Amref officially founded in 1957 to deliver mobile health services and surgical support to mission hospitals; a medical radio network developed to coordinate the service.

sources.title: Sir Michael Wood
sources.supports: Wood born in 1919, trained at Middlesex Hospital; chronic illness and his wife Sue's African roots prompting the move to Kenya in 1948; Wood flying himself to mission hospitals to operate; first professional pilot hired in 1961 while Wood kept flying his own plane.

sources.title: AMREF Flying Doctors celebrates 60 years in the air
sources.supports: In 1957 the three founders found that 75 per cent of the children they consulted in the region had burns; Wood had a farm on the slopes of Kilimanjaro and McIndoe co-owned the farm next to it; Rees an American reconstructive surgeon and former pupil of McIndoe's; the first aircraft a four-seater Piper Tri-Pacer flown by Wood; a starting budget of $14,000; the radio room 'Foundation Control' serving over 100 remote stations.

sources.title: Timeline
sources.supports: Founded in 1957 by the three reconstructive surgeons Michael Wood, Archibald McIndoe and Tom Rees on the foothills of Mount Kilimanjaro; outreach programme launched, initially servicing four hospitals in remote Kenya.

sources.title: History
sources.supports: 1956 plan by Wood, McIndoe and Rees born in the foothills of Mount Kilimanjaro; about one doctor for every 30,000 people in East Africa at the time; the founders saw an air-based service as the only way to reach remote communities; originally the African Medical Research Foundation, founded in 1957; medical radio network.

sources.title: Africa-Style 'House Calls' Saving Lives (Los Angeles Times, 10 March 1978, David Lamb)
sources.publisher: Los Angeles Times; scanned copy in the Amref Health Africa institutional repository
sources.supports: Wood, 59, piloting a single-engine plane from Nairobi to a Maasai settlement; his quotation 'you go to your patients. If you wait for them to come to you, they simply die'; the idea conceived 22 years earlier by Wood and Rees on a farm near Kilimanjaro, also nurtured by the late Sir Archibald McIndoe; the East African Flying Doctors Service, Nairobi-based and supported largely by private donations.

sources.title: Daktari (interview with Dr Thomas Rees about his memoir)
sources.supports: In 1957 three plastic surgeons began what was then called the Flying Doctors Service of Africa, using light aircraft to reach remote areas; McIndoe invited Rees to Africa; McIndoe and Wood among the starters of the service; Rees the sole surviving founder in 2003.

sources.title: Mansoor S. Emam, MD '90, & Thomas D. Rees, MD '48, Recipients of 2012 Distinguished Humanitarian Award
sources.publisher: University of Utah Spencer Fox Eccles School of Medicine (6 April 2012)
sources.supports: Rees trained in plastic surgery including a fellowship at Queen Victoria Hospital (East Grinstead), practised in New York, and was a founder and surgeon of the Flying Doctors Service of East Africa and AMREF.

research_notes: Dates: Amref's founders page and Amref Canada date the first conversation to 1956, and the 1978 Los Angeles Times piece says the idea came '22 years ago' (1956) over a bottle of Scotch on a farm near Kilimanjaro; all sources date the founding to 1957. The story keeps both dates. Name: VOA calls the 1957 body 'The Flying Doctors Service of Africa', Amref Canada 'the African Medical Research Foundation', the LA Times 'East African Flying Doctors Service', and later sources AMREF (renamed Amref Health Africa); the story says it founded 'the organisation that became the African Medical and Research Foundation, whose flying arm was known as the Flying Doctors'. One Wikipedia mirror says the organisation was registered in New York in 1957; no source read here confirms it, so it is not used. Money: the Flying Doctors' 2017 article gives a starting budget of $14,000; Amref's founders page gives 1960 expenditure of £11,500. They refer to different years and the story gives each with its year and attribution. The 75 per cent burns figure and the one-doctor-per-30,000 ratio each come from one Amref source and are attributed. The LA Times article is cited from the scanned PDF linked from the Amref repository record (https://repository.amref.ac.ke/bitstreams/12b4afcb-f333-4107-b10d-9cd4b69cc7e2/download); its OCR is poor, but the quoted sentence is legible, and the story quotes only from 'you go to your patients' to keep under 25 words. The Ol Orien farm is not said by any source to belong to a particular founder; the story says only that the conversation happened there and that Wood and McIndoe had neighbouring farms on the mountain. The New York Times obituaries of Wood (1987) and Rees (2013) block automated requests and were not used. A search result page contained an unrelated instruction about cooking, which was ignored. The Ben Sira line is general counsel about visiting the sick, applied here by analogy.
